world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Rottland, Franz. 1982. Die suednilotischen Sprachen: Beschreibung, Vergleichung und Rekonstruktion. Berlin: Reimer (covers Kalenjin varieties incl. Tugen); Kenyan IR theses on Tugen phonology unreachable.

new_statements.quote: Tucker/Bryan und Tucker sprechen in allen Arbeiten zum Kalenjin von 'stressed syllables', 'shift in stress' usw.; der Druckakzent scheint aber nach ihren Angaben mit Hochton oder Steigton korreliert zu sein, und markiert werden bei ihnen nur die Tonhöhen. [...] Bei meinen Aufzeichnungen habe ich keine Anzeichen für Druckakzent in phonemischer Funktion feststellen können und bezeichne ihn deshalb nicht. Phonetisch sind betonte Silben erkennbar, und zwar immer in Verbindung mit nicht-tiefem Ton.
new_statements.translation: Tucker/Bryan and Tucker speak in all their works on Kalenjin of 'stressed syllables', 'shift in stress', etc.; but by their own account the stress accent seems to be correlated with high or rising tone, and they mark only the pitch levels. [...] In my recordings I could find no sign of stress accent in a phonemic function, and therefore I do not mark it. Phonetically, stressed syllables are recognisable, and always in conjunction with non-low tone.
new_statements.citation: Rottland, Franz. 1982. Die südnilotischen Sprachen: Beschreibung, Vergleichung und Rekonstruktion (Kölner Beiträge zur Afrikanistik 7). Berlin: Dietrich Reimer. Ch. 5 'Kalenjin', sec. 5.1.3 'Prosodische Erscheinungen', 5.1.3.2 'Druckakzent'.
new_statements.locator: sec. 5.1.3.2 Druckakzent, p.78 (5.1.3 begins p.77 per the table of contents; the printed '78' falls a few lines into 5.1.3.3)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kalenjin (Tugen included) is a tone language (H/L; Jerono 2011 for Tugen). Rottland finds no phonemic word stress; a phonetic prominence is audible and always sits on a syllable bearing a non-low (high or falling) tone, i.e. stress, where heard, is a correlate of tone rather than an independent positional rule. No source gives a syllable-position rule for Tugen.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Rottland notes that in Heine's Sogoo (Okiek) vocabulary stress and tone are marked independently, stress going with high or falling tone but 'otherwise not predictable' — that remark concerns Sogoo, not Tugen. Tugen-specific sources: Jerono 2011:36-37 'Tugen is a tonal language... However, Tugen is not a typical tone language in that not every lexeme has different tones' (silent on stress); Lodge 1995:31 (Tugen informant) 'Kalenjin is a tone language' (silent on stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Rottland's remark concerns word-level 'Druckakzent' in isolated forms from his own recordings across Kalenjin varieties; it names no domain explicitly. It is a pan-Kalenjin statement in a comparative monograph, not a Tugen-specific one, and its text here is re-assembled from six overlapping Google Books API snippets (verbatim, but no page image). Tugen-specific descriptions (Jerono 2011 ch. 2; Lodge 1995; Local & Lodge 1996) are consistent with it: tone language, stress never mentioned.
new_statements.identity_note: The stress statement is Rottland 1982's pan-Kalenjin one (ch. 5 'Kalenjin' describes the whole Kalenjin cluster; Tugen = Rottland's 'Tugen/Tukin/Tugin, Kamasia', p.21), not a Tugen-only description; Tugen-specific sources (Jerono 2011, Lodge 1995 with a Tugen informant, Local & Lodge 1996 with Tugen speakers) describe a H/L tone language and never mention stress. Jerono 2011 treats Tugen as 'one of the dialects within the Kalenjin macro-language'; Lodge 1995 calls it 'the Tugen dialect' of Kalenjin. Glottolog language-level code tuge1241 [tuy]. The catalog already carries the sister language Nandi (nand1266) on Hollis 1909 + Lodge 1995; the Rottland passage applies to that entry as well.

sources.citation: Jerono, Prisca. 2011. Tugen Word Order: A Minimalist Perspective. PhD thesis, University of Nairobi (Linguistics), 172 pp. + front matter.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.note: Ch. 2 has 2.1 Consonants (p.31), 2.2 Vowels (p.33), 2.3 Tone (pp.36-37): 'Tugen is a tonal language in the sense that tone is used to differentiate lexical items... However, Tugen is not a typical tone language in that not every lexeme has different tones'; two underlying tones H and L, downstep, super-H, case marked by tone. The words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the thesis.

sources.citation: Lodge, Ken. 1995. Kalenjin phonology and morphology: A further exemplification of underspecification and non-destructive phonology. Lingua 96: 29-43.
sources.note: Tugen data (p.29: 'I shall concentrate on the Tugen dialect, that of my informant, Margaret Muthwii'). p.31: 'Kalenjin is a tone language, but whether the tonal system interacts with the harmony system is not clear, so I have not included tonal markings in the transcriptions'. No stress statement (only 'it must be stressed that', p.29).
